news_coverage.title: City hall to parents: Don't buy kids e-scooters for Christmas | London Free Press
news_coverage.summary: “While they can be fun to ride, e-scooters are not toys,” city officials said in a statement. The statement also quoted Shawna Chambers, city hall’s director of climate change, environment and waste management. “We have heard from a number of concerned residents that they see children riding e-scooters in their neighbourhoods,” Chambers said. “As we get closer to the holiday season, we want to make sure parents are aware of the legal and safety requirements for riding an e-scooter. “It is not an appropriate gift for children under 16.” In a recent 8-7 vote, city council approved extending for another six months a pilot project that allows e-scooters and power-assisted cargo bikes on city streets, with the province also recently extending its own pilot project allowing cities to regulate them. The city opted into the province’s e-scooter pilot program in 2023, allowing them for personal use with specific rules but barring e-scooter rental companies within London. Rules for e-scooters include barring riders younger than 16, not riding on sidewalks, not operating on roads with a speed limit greater than 50 kilometres/hour, not riding faster than 24 km/h, and not carrying passengers or cargo. \\ City council rejects ban, keeps e-scooters and cargo e-bikes on road 2. \\ From rules to risks: What you need to know about riding e-scooters London is taking part in the provincial e-scooter pilot until May 26, 2026, to see if existing rules work well. news_coverage.title: Committee backs major urban boundary growth amid First Nation concerns | London Free Press
news_coverage.summary: (Mike Hensen/The London Free Press) Despite resistance from a local First Nation, London politicians have endorsed a final version of the city’s urban boundary expansion – with a small addition. Politicians mostly expressed their desire to end a process that has dragged on for nearly two years and open more land for housing to meet London’s forecast population growth over the next 30-plus years. “We’re not rushing this, folks. We have had consultation,” Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis said. “When it leaves council, it goes to (Queen’s Park). They have to review it, they have to approve it, and they too have a duty to consult with our local First Nation communities. “Our job is to make a decision, and I’m quite comfortable with the decision we’ve got before us right now.” Lewis, Mayor Josh Morgan, and councillors Steve Lehman, Peter Cuddy, Susan Stevenson and Steven Hillier voted in favour of expanding the boundary. The urban boundary dictates where development can occur within the city’s borders. The proposed expansion – based on 2024 Queen’s Park population projections for 2051 that have since been revised down by about 55,000 people – would allow new development mostly in London’s northwest and west ends. Development stakeholders, including London Development Institute head Mike Wallace, supported the final map, stressing the expansion won’t trigger immediate construction. \\ Elbow room: By how much should London grow its urban boundary? 2. \\ Sprawling concerns: On London's edges, how many homes is too many? “This is a 30-year plan. The current urban growth boundary is over 30 years old,” Wallace said, adding that council can control the speed of growth. Holding up the map of the expansion, he added: “If you take this to your neighbours, I will gamble that they will say, ‘Well, that’s not much for 30 years.’” A map shows proposed additions to London’s urban growth boundary (yellow and red, highlighted in pink) and new industrial lands (blue), with natural heritage areas...

news_coverage.title: Push to strengthen London’s renoviction bylaw stalls after tie vote | London Free Press
news_coverage.summary: (Derek Ruttan/The London Free Press) A proposal to explore closing loopholes in London’s renoviction bylaw failed on a tie vote Monday, despite pleas from several tenants facing eviction to strengthen protections. They argued that because the bylaw focuses only on so-called renovictions, bad-faith landlords can simply issue an N13 that isn’t tied to renovations to avoid the licensing process. “When you’re involved in a controversy like this with your landlord. you never go to the (Landlord and Tenant Board) and you’re told, ‘You won, congratulations, it’s over,’ ” Trosow said. “They can come back and do it again and again. And if they don’t want to use the same tactic they used unsuccessfully the first time, they’ve got a variety of different things they can do.” Trosow and Ferreira voted in favour of the motion at Monday’s community and protective services committee meeting, while councillors Jerry Pribil and Elizabeth Peloza voted against it. Evictions for renovations or repairs are legal under provincial rules, but critics say they’re often used to remove long-term tenants so a unit can be re-listed at a far higher market rate. London’s bylaw – one of the first in the province – requires landlords planning major renovation work that needs a unit vacated to apply for a $600 licence within seven days of serving tenants with an N13 eviction notice. City hall says seven licences have been issued so far. \\ Renoviction bylaw sees zero applications, but new eviction trend emerges 2. \\ London has a new 'renoviction' bylaw: Here's how it works To obtain a licence, landlords must submit a report from an engineer or architect confirming the renovation requires the unit to be empty. news_coverage.summary: David Ferreira speaks at London city hall on Wednesday November 26, 2025. (Mike Hensen/The London Free Press) Two London city councillors are looking to close what they view as loopholes in the city’s “renoviction” bylaw, which has seen little uptake since being introduced earlier this year. While evictions for renovations or repairs are legal under provincial rules, critics argue it is a common tactic to remove long-term tenants and re-list a unit at a much higher market rate. Downtown councillor David Ferreira said loopholes are being exploited through that bylaw, including eviction for the purpose of demolition or conversion to a non-residential use, which does not require the licence. How can we integrate it into the program that we currently have? Hopefully there’s no additional cost for us. to have more tools, more protection mechanisms for tenants,” Ferreira said, adding there’s only been a handful of licences issued. He cited an example in his own ward of four seniors under the same roof, which recently changed ownership, who he says were issued multiple N13 eviction notices for the purpose of converting their units into commercial space. \\ Renoviction bylaw sees zero applications, but new eviction trend emerges 2. \\ London has a new 'renoviction' bylaw: Here's how it works Ferreira criticized the move, saying there’s more than enough commercial space around the core-area building. news_coverage.title: City council finalizes 3.4% tax hike, adds one-time rental relief | London Free Press
news_coverage.summary: Hadleigh McAlister talks about Salvation Army funding in the city budget after deliberations wrapped up Wednesday, Nov. (Mike Hensen/The London Free Press) Londoners will face a 3.4 per cent property tax hike next year, a figure that includes a new addition of temporary rental assistance as part of the city budget finalized Wednesday. The funding will go toward financial assistance for low-income Londoners for rent and utilities to help them retain housing. Budget chair Elizabeth Peloza was absent. The increase won’t move the needle on next year’s now-final tax hike, which represents a $51 increase for every $100,000 in a home’s assessed property value. “No, I’m not going to veto any of the changes council made,” he said, promising a formal declaration Thursday. “I do have the ability to waive my veto period to basically no time at all, and then that essentially will end the budget process.” The 2026 budget update initially began at a forecasted 6.4 per cent tax hike at the end of last year’s talks. Right-sizing by city hall and some of its agencies, plus surplus money injected to lower taxes, contributed to the final tally. Among the biggest additions are $2.3 million to help pay off office relocation debt for the Middlesex-London Health Unit, and $784,000 to provide two free hours of on-street parking in London’s core. Both the health unit and London Middlesex Community Housing are also receiving more than $600,000 each to help address funding gaps. Several attempts were made during budget deliberations to increase funding for the Housing Stability Bank that already receives $1.3 million annually from the city. news_coverage.title: City council rejects ban, keeps e-scooters and cargo e-bikes on road | London Free Press
news_coverage.summary: (Derek Ruttan/The London Free Press) London politicians narrowly voted in favour of continuing to allow the use of electric scooters and cargo bikes on city streets, as several spoke of neighbourhood concerns about their misuse. Failure to pass that vote would have meant the immediate banning of e-scooters and cargo “power-assisted” bikes in London. “I think banning them as of tonight. is frankly horrible, when people spent thousands of dollars, especially on (cargo e-bikes) to be able to choose that as their method of transportation,” she said. “A lot of people are actually using these to get to work and to school.” Councillors Corrine Rahman, Peter Cuddy, Paul Van Meerbergen, Steven Hillier, Shawn Lewis, Steve Lehman and Susan Stevenson voted against continuing the pilot, while all others voted in favour. The city opted into the province’s e-scooter pilot program in 2023, allowing for personal use with specific rules but barring e-scooter rental companies from operating in London. Rules include not riding on sidewalks, not operating on roads with a speed limit greater than 50 kilometres per hour, barring riders under the age of 16, and requiring those under 18 to wear a helmet. Both Lewis and Rahman spoke of concerns from residents about scofflaws and the difficulty for those residents to report issues and for city bylaw to follow up. \\ London boy advocates for helmet use after injuries in e-scooter crash 2. \\ Ride or wrong? City hall seeks input on e-scooters, cargo e-bikes “At this point, the onus is on residents to report a scooter that they saw flying by them usually at a high rate of speed with no way to differentiate one from the other,” Rahman said. “When residents in my ward have tried to complain. they were told to follow the e-scooter home.” Franke’s motion will allow staff to generate a report and gather public feedback on the pilot before it expires. news_coverage.summary: (Mike Hensen/The London Free Press) Politicians have given their approval to demolish a more than 150-year-old farmhouse in Hyde Park in order to build apartments, going against a city staff recommendation. “I certainly understand the desire for development in this area, I certainly know the character and history of the (building),” said Mayor Josh Morgan, a former neighbouring Ward 7 councillor. “If (the developer wants) to draw the public in though, it’s my strong encouragement that you. preserve some of the components of the building that I think could make very unique and interesting features within a new build.” Both votes Tuesday went against city staff recommendations, which sought heritage designation for the property and sought to deny the development proposal from North Development Corp. based both on heritage concerns and the proposal exceeding the eight-storey height limit. Councillors Anna Hopkins, Skylar Franke, David Ferreira, Elizabeth Peloza and Sam Trosow opposed denying heritage designation for the building, while all others voted in support. “Heritage designation, in my opinion is very warranted. (it’s) one of the few protections that the community has from the loss of these historic and irreplaceable heritage aspects,” Trosow said. \\ Should this 1870s-built house, now a restaurant, be razed for apartments? 2. \\ City politicians buck staff advice, refuse heritage tag for 1870s-era building On the planning application, Coun. Corrine Rahman joined Hopkins, Trosow, and Peloza in voting against the rezoning granting the density and height, and Franke, Hopkins, Ferreira, Peloza, and Trosow voted against everything else. Under provincial heritage rules, for a property to receive designation it must meet at least two of nine criteria for architectural and historical significance. news_coverage.title: London budget: Why city council is covering health unit moving debt | London Free Press
news_coverage.summary: (Derek Ruttan/The London Free Press) London city council has shown its support for helping pay off the Middlesex-London Health Unit’s relocation debt, turning the page on what has been a tumultuous chapter for the public health authority amid a budget crunch. LFP’s Jack Moulton reports. Public health offices are in charge of disease prevention and vaccination campaigns, inspections for food-serving businesses, as well as other health programs including sexual health and addiction. The funding breakdown for the health unit works out to 70 per cent from Queen’s Park, and based on population, 25 per cent from London and five per cent from Middlesex County. WHAT IS CITY HALL’S PLAN? Included in Mayor Josh Morgan’s 2026 budget update and so far endorsed by city council is a proposal for London to chip in $2.3 million to help pay off the health unit’s debt from its move from its former building at 50 King St. to downtown’s Citi Plaza mall five years ago. That proposal kicked off the longest debate among politicians during budget talks last week, with councillors Skylar Franke and Susan Stevenson seeking to remove said pitch from the budget, arguing it absolves the province of their share. “I’m not very supportive of that, in that 70 per cent of that debt is the province’s,” said Franke, who sits on the health unit board. “The reason there is a loan in the first place is because the province would not provide capital funding.” The idea behind the move was to free up the roughly $241,000 the health unit pays annually in principle and interest payments toward the loan for the next 10 years, so that some of the funding can go back into the health unit’s operations. \\ Cost-cutting health unit set to shut down main office in Strathroy 2. \\ Inside London’s 2026 budget: Tax relief, road repairs and health unit debt In a letter to politicians, health unit chief executive Emily Williams outlined how they are the second-lowest funded public health office in the province per capita...

news_coverage.summary: (Mike Hensen/The London Free Press) Business leaders are thrilled to see London pledge a return to two hours of free parking in the city’s core, just as studies continue into a new strategy for the downtown. Play Video The city has almost continuously had some element of free parking through the Honk app in the core since the pandemic, and with commercial vacancies still high, some politicians sought to ensure more stability. “If we are wanting to revitalize the downtown. this is what it is, just small little moves that we can make that allow us to open up the downtown for the city at large,” Ferreira said. “If someone’s coming for an appointment, one hour is not enough, if someone is coming for a lunch, one hour is too tight.” The motion was approved 11-4 with councillors Skylar Franke, Corrine Rahman, Elizabeth Peloza, and Sam Trosow opposed, while all others voted in support. The extension of the Honk app promotion allowing for free on-street parking, recently brought down from two hours to one, was one of the “quick start” actions recommended and approved until the end of the year through the early drafting stages of the new downtown plan. Politicians got a glimpse of the next stage of the new plan, a blueprint for revitalizing the city’s core, last week and endorsed exploring another set of moves.
